summary: Documents BSD rlogin, which provides a remote-echoed, locally flow-controlled virtual terminal with proper flushing of output. It describes an existing widely used protocol and is informational. It was replaced by RFC 1282.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1258 documents BSD rlogin, a TCP-based remote terminal facility. It describes connection setup, flow-control modes, window-size updates, and control messages.

subtitle: A BSD remote-terminal protocol with local flow control and terminal-size updates.

tldr.problem: A remote terminal connection may need Unix terminal behavior such as local flow control, window-size updates, and flushing buffered output.
tldr.mechanism: BSD rlogin runs over TCP, exchanges user and terminal information, supports cooked and raw modes, and carries control bytes for flushing or changing modes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1258 documents an existing protocol and was obsoleted by RFC 1282.

today: RFC 1258 is an Informational document that was obsoleted by RFC 1282. It records the BSD rlogin protocol and its security cautions.

sections.title: A Remote Terminal with Unix Semantics
sections.content: Rlogin provides a remote-echoed, locally flow-controlled virtual terminal and proper flushing of output. It uses TCP port 513 and assumes an eight-bit transparent stream. The RFC documents a commonly implemented protocol rather than specifying an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Rlogin connects a local terminal to a remote host and carries terminal data over TCP. The protocol includes ways to manage output and terminal behavior.

sections.title: Setting Up a Connection
sections.content: At connection start, the client sends four null-terminated strings: an empty string, the client user name, the server user name, and terminal type and speed. The server replies with a zero byte to indicate it has received the strings and entered data-transfer mode. Window-size negotiation may follow.
sections.plainLanguage: The client first sends identity and terminal information. The server's zero-byte reply marks the start of data transfer.

sections.title: Flow Control and Window Updates
sections.content: In cooked mode, the client intercepts START and STOP characters to control remote output locally. In raw mode, it sends those characters to the server. If supported, the server can receive a 12-byte window-size sequence with row, column, and pixel dimensions; server control bytes can also flush buffered output or switch modes.
sections.plainLanguage: Cooked mode handles start and stop locally; raw mode sends those characters to the remote host. The client can also report changes to its window size.

sections.title: The Trusted-Host Warning
sections.content: The RFC warns that rlogin may be configured to allow passwordless login from trusted hosts. If one system in that trust relationship is compromised, other systems that accept it may also be exposed. The document also notes that host-name trust can be undermined by compromise of the domain name server or the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Passwordless login from trusted hosts is convenient but risky. If one trusted system is compromised, other systems that trust it may also be at risk.
